title: Who moves the mind?
hookLine: a student asks who moves the mind; the Kena answers: Brahman
carry: brahman is the one the mind runs on
last: UNCOVER IT, SO I MAY SEE.

cards: Long ago, a student sat down near his teacher. That's one old meaning of the word Upanishad: sitting down near. He didn't ask for a blessing or a rule.
He asked the question small children ask in bed, right before grown-ups teach them to stop: who's thinking my thoughts? The teacher didn't laugh it off.
He answered, and the answer became a whole Upanishad, named after the student's first word. Kena. By whom?

teach.h: BY WHOM DOES THE MIND FLY OUT?
teach.b: Here is the question, the first verse. By whom willed, by whom sent, does the mind fly out to its objects? By whom commanded does the first breath move?
By whom impelled do people speak? What god sets the eye and the ear to work? Mind, breath, speech, eye, ear: the things you'd call you.
And notice: you didn't order your next thought. It arrived. You don't decide to breathe; it breathes.
So who is doing the doing? The teacher's answer, unfolding all week, is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: Brahman. You've met the word.
It's the tradition's name for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. And the Kena says Brahman isn't far off, past the sky.

teach.h: BRAHMAN: WHAT THE MIND RUNS ON.
teach.b: It's the one your mind runs on, so close the mind can't grab it, the way a hand can't grab itself. This isn't only for philosophers.
Many teachers hear the same idea in the prayer you met on day three, the Gayatri, which many Hindus say every morning.

teach.h: GAYATRI: MAY IT MOVE OUR MINDS.
teach.b: Its last line asks the divine light: may it move our minds, may it set our thinking going.

teach.h: BRAHMAN IS THE ONE THE MIND RUNS ON.
teach.b: The Kena asks: by whom is the mind sent out? The Gayatri asks that light, at sunrise, to be the one who sends it. So on the nights a mind won't stop, the Hindu answer isn't only: calm down.
It's: your racing mind isn't the boss here. Something deeper moves it, and you can ask that something to steer.

how: The Kena's opening question, 'kena?', by whom?, is a classic starting point for self-inquiry in Vedanta. Many Hindus say the Gayatri mantra each morning; its last line asks the divine light to move, or inspire, our minds.

games.q: a student asks: by whom is the mind sent out? what do you expect the teacher to say?
o: 'by the one the mind itself runs on.'
games.why: the Kena takes the question seriously: behind mind, breath and speech is Brahman, which the mind can't grab.

practice: Close your eyes and wait for the next thought without making one. When it comes, notice you didn't order it; it arrived. If you pray, say the Gayatri's meaning softly: may the light move my mind.
If you don't, hold the Kena's question instead, not to answer it, just to hold it: by whom? Rest in the gap between thoughts.

wordCard.voice: Kena, by whom? The question that opens this Upanishad: by whom does the mind fly out to its objects, by whom does the first breath move?

orig.note: Sanskrit: kena, by whom?; the Upanishad's first word and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman is the one the mind runs on. Tomorrow the teacher answers. See you then.
